## Answer

The statement is **false** in general. I provide a counterexample.

### Counterexample

Let $G = \mathbb{R}$ (the real numbers under addition, with the standard Euclidean topology) and $H = \mathbb{Z}$ (the integers, a subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$).

**Compute $G/H$.** The quotient $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ is the set of cosets $x + \mathbb{Z}$. The map
$$\varphi: \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow S^1, \qquad x + \mathbb{Z} \longmapsto e^{2\pi i x}$$
is a well-defined homeomorphism (it is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space, hence a homeomorphism; or equivalently, one checks directly that it is open). Thus
$$G/H \;\cong\; S^1.$$

**Compute $H$.** The subgroup $H = \mathbb{Z}$ carries the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}$, which is the **discrete** topology (every singleton $\{n\}$ is open, being $\mathbb{Z} \cap (n - \tfrac{1}{2},\, n + \tfrac{1}{2})$).

**Therefore**
$$G/H \times H \;\cong\; S^1 \times \mathbb{Z}_{\text{disc}} \;=\; \bigsqcup_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \bigl(S^1 \times \{n\}\bigr),$$
i.e., a topological disjoint union of **countably infinitely many** copies of the circle $S^1$.

### Why $G/H \times H \not\simeq G$

- **$G = \mathbb{R}$ is connected.** It has exactly **one** connected component.
- **$G/H \times H \cong S^1 \times \mathbb{Z}_{\text{disc}}$ is totally disconnected between its slices.** Each slice $S^1 \times \{n\}$ is a connected component (it is connected, being homeomorphic to $S^1$, and it is both open and closed in the product since $\{n\}$ is clopen in the discrete topology). Hence $G/H \times H$ has **countably infinitely many** connected components.

A homeomorphism is a bijection that preserves all topological structure, and in particular it induces a bijection between the sets of connected components. A space with one connected component cannot be homeomorphic to a space with countably infinitely many connected components.

$$\boxed{G/H \times H \;\not\simeq\; G.}$$

### When the statement *does* hold

The isomorphism $G/H \times H \simeq G$ holds under the additional hypothesis that the quotient map $\pi: G \to G/H$ admits a **continuous section** $s: G/H \to G$ (a continuous map with $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}$) that is also a **group homomorphism**—equivalently, when $G$ is (topologically and algebraically) a **semidirect product** $G \cong H \rtimes (G/H)$. In that case the map
$$H \times G/H \longrightarrow G, \qquad (h, \bar{g}) \longmapsto h \cdot s(\bar{g})$$
is a homeomorphism and a group isomorphism. But such a section need not exist in general, as the counterexample above shows: there is no continuous group-theoretic section $S^1 \to \mathbb{R}$ of the covering map $\mathbb{R} \to S^1$ (any such section would be a continuous homomorphism from the compact group $S^1$ into the torsion-free group $\mathbb{R}$, which must be trivial—contradicting the section property).

### Conclusion

The statement $G/H \times H \simeq G$ is **not true** for an arbitrary subgroup $H \leq G$ of a topological group. The pair $(G, H) = (\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z})$ furnishes an explicit counterexample: $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} \cong S^1 \times \mathbb{Z}_{\text{disc}}$ has countably many connected components, whereas $\mathbb{R}$ is connected, so the two spaces are not homeomorphic.

### PROOF COMPLETE
